content: Regular physical activity is associated with improved overall health and a decreased risk of all-cause mortality and the development of numerous chronic diseases in adults. Despite this, many adults remain sedentary or engage in less physical activity than recommended. Children and adolescents are generally more active than adults, but their participation in physical activity tends to decline significantly during adolescence. Schools and community programs have the potential to help young people establish lifelong, healthy physical activity habits. This report outlines recommendations to encourage physical activity among young people, aiming to ensure they continue to engage in such activities into adulthood and reap the associated health benefits throughout their lives. The guidelines were developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in collaboration with experts from universities, national organizations, federal agencies, and voluntary groups. These recommendations are based on a thorough review of research, theoretical frameworks, and current practices in physical education, exercise science, health education, and public health. Physical Activity, Exercise, and Physical Fitness It is important to distinguish between physical activity, exercise, and physical fitness. Exercise is a subset of physical activity that is planned, structured, and repetitive, with the goal of improving or maintaining physical fitness. Physical fitness refers to a set of attributes that are either health-related (e.g., cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, and body composition) or skill-related (e.g., balance, agility, power, reaction time, speed, and coordination). Health Benefits of Physical Activity and Fitness Regular moderate physical activity provides numerous health benefits for adults, including improved cardiorespiratory endurance, flexibility, and muscular strength. It can also reduce obesity, alleviate depression and anxiety, and enhance bone mass density. Physically active adults are less likely to develop chronic diseases such as cardiovascular disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and colon cancer. Additionally, physically active individuals have lower all-cause mortality rates compared to sedentary individuals. For children and adolescents, regular physical activity improves aerobic endurance, muscular strength, and various health indicators such as body mass index, blood lipid profiles, and resting blood pressure. It is particularly important for young people with chronic disease risk factors, as it can lower blood pressure, improve physical fitness in obese children, and reduce the degree of overweight. Physical activity is also associated with higher self-esteem, better self-concept, and lower levels of anxiety and stress among adolescents. Weight-bearing exercises during youth may increase bone mass density, potentially reducing the risk of osteoporosis later in life. Recommended Physical Activity for Young People Increased awareness of the health benefits of physical activity has led to greater recognition of the need for initiatives to reduce sedentary lifestyles. It is recommended that children and adolescents engage in daily physical activity as part of play, games, sports, work, transportation, recreation, physical education, or planned exercise. Adolescents should participate in at least three sessions per week of activities lasting 20 minutes or more that require moderate to vigorous exertion. Prevalence of Physical Activity Among Young People Although children and adolescents are generally more active than adults, many do not meet the recommended levels of physical activity. For example, only 52% of high school girls and 74% of boys report engaging in vigorous exercise on at least three days in the past week. Physical activity levels decline steadily during adolescence, with only 38% of individuals aged 18–21 engaging in vigorous exercise compared to 69% of those aged 12–13. Factors Influencing Physical Activity Several factors influence physical activity levels among children and adolescents, including demographic, individual, interpersonal, and environmental factors. Girls are generally less active than boys, and older children and adolescents are less active than younger ones. Positive attitudes toward physical activity, enjoyment of such activities, and perceptions of competence are associated with higher activity levels. Conversely, barriers such as lack of time negatively impact physical activity participation. Interpersonal and environmental factors, such as support from peers, friends, and family, also play a significant role. Access to convenient play spaces, sports equipment, and transportation to fitness programs positively correlates with physical activity levels. Objectives for Physical Activity Among Young People National health promotion objectives aim to increase the proportion of young people engaging in regular physical activity and reduce the prevalence of overweight and sedentary behaviors. These objectives include increasing daily physical education participation, enhancing community access to fitness facilities, and ensuring healthcare providers routinely assess and counsel patients on physical activity. Rationale for School and Community Efforts Schools and communities play a critical role in promoting physical activity among young people. Many children already exhibit risk factors for chronic diseases, such as obesity, and physical activity has proven benefits for their physical and mental health. Schools are uniquely positioned to provide physical activity instruction and programs, as they reach most children and adolescents. Communities are essential for supporting physical activity outside the school setting. Coordinated efforts between schools and communities can maximize resources and promote lifelong physical activity habits. Recommendations for School and Community Programs 1. Policy Development: Establish policies that promote enjoyable, lifelong physical activity among young people. 2. Supportive Environments: Create physical and social environments that encourage safe and enjoyable physical activity. 3. Physical Education: Implement curricula that emphasize enjoyable participation and help students develop the skills and confidence needed for active lifestyles. 4. Health Education: Provide instruction that complements physical education and promotes knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors supporting physical activity. 5. Extracurricular Activities: Offer programs that cater to the diverse needs and interests of students. 6. Parental Involvement: Engage parents in physical activity programs and encourage their support for their children’s participation. 7. Personnel Training: Train educators, coaches, and healthcare providers to effectively promote physical activity. 8. Health Services: Assess and counsel young people on physical activity and refer them to appropriate programs. 9. Community Programs: Provide developmentally appropriate sports and recreation programs that appeal to all young people. 10. Evaluation: Regularly evaluate physical activity programs and facilities to ensure effectiveness. By implementing these recommendations, schools and communities can foster a culture of physical activity that benefits young people’s health and well-being throughout their lives.
